title: What Next for Qatar, Iran and the World's Largest Gas Field?
gist: Strikes in the 2026 Middle East conflict took roughly 4.5 bcfd of Qatari gas-processing capacity offline (about 17% of Qatar's LNG export capacity) and hit Iran's Assaluyeh hub, at a US$5.8 billion repair bill and recovery timelines of up to twelve months. Wood Mackenzie argues the episode converts a long-known geographic concentration risk on the shared North Field/South Pars structure into an operational reality across the whole value chain, just as 54 mmtpa of uncontracted Qatari volumes approach the market by 2035.

themes.theme: Shared supergiant = single point of failure

insights.claim: The North Field and South Pars form a single supergiant structure on the Qatar Arch spanning around 9,000 square kilometres and holding more than 2,200 tcf of remaining gas resources, 25% of the global total.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: A quarter of world gas reserves sits inside one contiguous, militarily exposed structure: the single largest tail risk embedded in global gas supply curves.
insights.quote: The North Field and South Pars hold more than 2,200 tcf of remaining gas resources, 25% of the global total

insights.claim: The combined Qatari-Iranian structure supplies 10% of global gas production, producing the equivalent of twice Europe's entire gas supply from one shared field complex.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Sizes the outage risk: any prolonged escalation on the Qatar Arch removes a volume that no combination of alternative suppliers can backfill quickly.
insights.quote: producing the equivalent of twice Europe's entire gas supply from a single shared structure spanning around 9,000 square kilometres

insights.claim: Qatar holds 85% of the shared North Field/South Pars resource, with 2P reserves of 275 tcf, against Iran's minority share.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Explains why Qatar monetises the field for export while Iran cannot: the resource split, not just sanctions, sets the strategic asymmetry.
insights.quote: Qatar holds 85% of the shared resource, with 2P reserves of 275 tcf.

insights.claim: The 2026 conflict turned a well-understood geographical concentration risk into an operational reality across the entire value chain, from wellhead to export terminal, rather than remaining a theoretical scenario in risk models.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Expect buyers and lenders to reprice Qatari supply-concentration risk explicitly in contract terms and portfolio diversification premiums.
insights.quote: What this conflict has done is turn a well-understood geographical concentration risk into an operational reality across the entire value chain, from wellhead to export terminal.

insights.claim: Damage from the strikes cascaded across the whole value chain rather than being confined to upstream wells, hitting production, LNG liquefaction and export infrastructure simultaneously.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Repair sequencing matters more than reserve size; liquefaction and export bottlenecks, not resource, will dictate the restart curve.
insights.quote: The damage has cascaded across the entire value chain, from upstream production through to LNG liquefaction and export infrastructure.

themes.theme: Qatari outage arithmetic and repair bill

insights.claim: Strikes on the Pearl GTL complex in March 2026 and an explosion at the Barzan gas plant in June 2026 removed around 4.5 billion cubic feet per day of gas-processing capacity, comprising two LNG trains totalling 12.7 mmtpa, one GTL train and Barzan's domestic lean-gas processing.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: A concrete 12.7 mmtpa hole in global LNG supply that tightens spot balances until trains return.
insights.quote: removed around 4.5 billion cubic feet per day (bcfd) of gas-processing capacity: two LNG trains totalling 12.7 million tonnes per annum (mmtpa), one GTL train, and Barzan's domestic lean-gas processing

insights.claim: The Qatari outages account for roughly 17% of Qatar's LNG export capacity.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: A near-one-fifth cut to the world's largest LNG exporter is a direct bullish input to JKM and TTF spreads while repairs run.
insights.quote: The outages account for roughly 17% of Qatar's LNG export capacity.

insights.claim: The Barzan shutdown alone removes 35% of Qatar's 4 bcfd domestic gas supply, creating an internal power and industrial feedstock problem alongside the export loss.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Domestic shortfall competes with export cargoes for molecules, so headline LNG export losses may understate the tightness.
insights.quote: The Barzan shutdown alone removes 35% of Qatar's 4 bcfd domestic gas supply.

insights.claim: Combined repair costs for the damaged Qatari facilities are estimated at US$5.8 billion in real terms, with recovery timelines running from four to twelve months.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: The four-to-twelve-month spread is the key tradeable uncertainty: the long end keeps LNG tight through a full winter.
insights.quote: Wood Mackenzie estimates combined repair costs at US$5.8 billion in real terms, with recovery timelines running from four to twelve months.

insights.claim: Around 10% of Shell's upstream cash flow is at risk from the Pearl GTL outage alone.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: The only named single-company earnings exposure in the piece: a direct, quantified downgrade vector for Shell's upstream cash flow guidance.
insights.quote: Around 10% of Shell's upstream cash flow is at risk from the Pearl GTL outage alone.

insights.claim: Qatar must execute US$5.8 billion of repairs with up to twelve-month recovery timelines at the same time as commissioning the largest LNG expansion programme in the world, straining the same engineering and contractor base.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Watch for expansion-project slippage as repair work competes for EPC capacity; delay risk to North Field start-ups is underpriced.
insights.quote: Qatar is managing US$5.8 billion in repairs and recovery timelines of up to twelve months while commissioning the largest LNG expansion programme in the world

insights.claim: Strikes on the Assaluyeh processing hub, which handles around 30% of South Pars output, and on Phase 13 facilities at Kangan have disrupted production across multiple field phases in Iran.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Processing hubs, not wells, are the chokepoint: a third of South Pars throughput hinges on one site.
insights.quote: Strikes on the Assaluyeh processing hub, which handles around 30% of South Pars output, and on Phase 13 facilities at Kangan have disrupted production across multiple field phases.

insights.claim: South Pars supplies 40-50% of Iran's fuel demand and around 80% of its power generation, making the field a domestic survival asset rather than an export earner.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Disruption translates into Iranian blackouts and industrial shutdowns, a domestic-stability variable that feeds geopolitical escalation risk.
insights.quote: South Pars supplies 40-50% of Iran's fuel demand and around 80% of its power generation.

insights.claim: Iran has no LNG export infrastructure and no meaningful energy diversification, so damage to South Pars cannot be monetised away or offset through alternative supply channels.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Unlike Qatar, Iran's loss does not show up in seaborne LNG balances, so traders should model it through oil products and regional escalation instead.
insights.quote: The country has no LNG export infrastructure, no meaningful energy diversification, and peak summer gas demand that surges to over 11 bcfd.

insights.claim: Iran relies on liquid fuels to cover any gas supply shortfall against peak summer gas demand that surges to over 11 bcfd, a gap the current disruption is widening.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Implies incremental Iranian fuel oil and distillate burn, tightening regional product balances and cutting exportable crude/product barrels.
insights.quote: Iran relies on liquid fuels to cover any supply shortfall, a gap the current disruption is widening.

themes.theme: Trade flows and the uncontracted LNG window

insights.claim: Qatar exported more than 80 million tonnes of LNG in 2025, with India receiving 11.9 million tonnes, Taiwan 8.2 million tonnes, and Europe accounting for just 11% of total supply.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Asia, not Europe, absorbs the first-order shock; Indian and Taiwanese buyers are the ones forced into spot procurement.
insights.quote: Qatar exported more than 80 million tonnes of LNG in 2025, with India receiving 11.9 million tonnes, Taiwan 8.2 million tonnes, and Europe accounting for just 11% of total supply.

insights.claim: North Field East, North Field South and North Field West were set to add a combined 48 mmtpa of new liquefaction capacity and lift plateau production to 28 bcfd by 2033.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: This 48 mmtpa wave is the single biggest determinant of late-2020s LNG oversupply; slippage flips the 2030 balance from loose to tight.
insights.quote: North Field East, North Field South, and North Field West were set to add a combined 48 mmtpa of new liquefaction capacity and lift plateau production to 28 bcfd by 2033

insights.claim: Wood Mackenzie expects 54 mmtpa of uncontracted Qatari volumes to reach the market by 2035, while buyers are making long-term security decisions right now.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: The mismatch between a huge uncontracted overhang and buyers signing today is the core commercial tension: contract pricing and duration should move in buyers' favour only if restoration is fast.
insights.quote: 54 mmtpa of uncontracted Qatari volumes will reach the market by 2035, and buyers are making long-term security decisions right now

insights.claim: The pace of infrastructure restoration will directly shape how the Qatari contracting window develops and how buyers weigh their long-term supply security options.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Track repair milestones as a leading indicator of Qatari contract terms and of whether buyers diversify toward US and other suppliers.
insights.quote: The pace of infrastructure restoration will now directly shape how that contracting window develops and how buyers weigh their long-term supply security options.

insights.claim: Qatar's North Field underpins a downstream industrial complex spanning condensate refining, NGLs, methanol, ammonia and gas-to-liquids output, so the outage propagates well beyond LNG.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Look for second-order squeezes in methanol and ammonia chains, not just gas, when modelling the conflict's commodity impact.
insights.quote: Qatar's North Field underpins a downstream industrial complex that includes condensate refining, NGLs, methanol, ammonia, and gas-to-liquids output.

insights.claim: The field supplies around one-third of global helium demand, concentrating a critical industrial gas in the same disrupted geography.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Helium is a thinly traded, semiconductor- and medical-critical input; a third of demand exposed to one conflict zone is an under-watched squeeze candidate.
insights.quote: It also supplies around one-third of global helium demand

insights.claim: Qatari output produces sulphur feeding international industrial and agricultural markets, linking the gas disruption to fertiliser input chains.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Adds a fertiliser-cost transmission channel from a Gulf gas outage into food-inflation models.
insights.quote: produces sulphur feeding international industrial and agricultural markets

insights.claim: Qatar hosts the world's largest post-FID Carbon Capture, Utilization and Storage development at Ras Laffan, targeting around 11 mmtpa of CO2 capture.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Qatari LNG's carbon-intensity pitch to European and Asian buyers rests on this project; delays weaken its low-carbon marketing edge.
insights.quote: Qatar hosts the world's largest post-FID Carbon Capture, Utilization, and Storage development at Ras Laffan, targeting around 11 mmtpa of CO2 capture
